articles.title: China has cracked down on AI relationships. Is it ahead of the game?
articles.summary: Beijing has cracked down on AI chatbots that can replicate human relationships. Experts are asking if this is the right thing to do.
articles.full_text:
By Stephanie Hegarty ,  Global population correspondent   and   Wanqing Zhang ,  Global China Unit 
In early 2024, a young man in the city of Huangshi, south-eastern China, reportedly posted a message on the Chinese version of TikTok, Douyin. The caption read: "Farewell to this world." 
Within minutes, the suicide prevention team at Douyin kicked into gear. The team, which is staffed 24 hours a day, shared the man's posts with five police stations in Huangshi. 
After geolocating one of his videos to a local park, police found him in emotional distress and intervened before he was able to take his own life. 
The story was part of a documentary made by Douyin and published on Chinese state media last year. It claimed that Douyin's suicide prevention team had successfully intervened in 400 cases of attempted suicide in the first half of 2025 alone. 
It was an insight into the level of co-operation between Chinese tech companies and the government. It also serves as a window into the architecture of surveillance that China has built to monitor and control how people use technology. 
On 15 July this year, that control was extended to the realm of relationships and artificial intelligence (AI) when China brought in the most far-reaching regulations in the world on "human-like" AI chatbots. 
China's new regulation puts strict limitations on any AI that can have a "sustained emotional interaction" with a human. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Xi and Trump met last week 
US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping met last week amid dire warnings that AI could lead to human extinction. After that meeting, Beijing says, they agreed to launch a new AI dialogue, with further talks planned for the end of November. 
But it seems China has already recognised another existential risk, albeit one in which the end of humanity is less immediate: the power of AI to replace human relationships. 
Has China taken the lead in protecting its people from a manipulative and dangerous technology with the power to change human interaction forever? Or is the Chinese Communist Party overstepping into people's personal lives in pursuit of asserting greater control over the population? 
'Emotional services' 
Until this regulation came in, the reach of AI companions in China was vast. 
There are about 128 million monthly active users of AI companion apps outside of China, according to the market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. Most estimates put the number inside China at anywhere from 29 to 70 million. 
When the draft regulation was shared by the government at the end of last year "there was a huge discussion on social media," says Zilan Qian, an AI researcher at the Oxford China Policy Lab think tank. "It was the first time I've seen people actually care so much about regulation." 
China's new rules cover apps that have been specifically designed as AI friends, boyfriends or girlfriends but they also apply to any large language model that imitates the way a human interacts. 
The wording of the regulation is vague. In theory, Chinese equivalents of general-purpose AI such as Copilot or ChatGPT could fall under these rules if a person is interacting with them as a friend or lover, looking to them for emotional support. And many people do this. 
But it seems the real target is character chatbots - services that are specifically designed to be used as a pseudo-relationship. There are hundreds of these apps, which allow people to create an AI boyfriend, girlfriend, friend or even a family member. 
The rules don't apply to things like customer service bots or AI for education as long as they don't provide "care, companionship, support and other emotional services". 
For children, the regulation is clearest. Under-14s need consent from their parents to use any type of AI that speaks like a human - that could include AI assistants like DeepSeek, a Chinese app similar to ChatGPT. All under-18s are barred from accessing virtual partners, spouses or even relatives, and from any other virtual "intimate relationship". 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Police work closely with social media firms in China 
For adults, it is not a hard ban, but it is restrictive, even if some of the wording is ambiguous. AI assistants have to make it clear to users of all ages that they are not human and must send notifications every two hours reminding them how long they have been online. 
Chatbots can't create "emotional reliance or addiction" or induce people to make "unreasonable decisions". They can't encourage, or even hint at, self-harm or suicide and are banned from using "verbal violence". 
Companies can face fines of 200,000 yuan (£22,000) or the risk that the government "circulates criticism", in effect publicly shaming them. 
A week before the law came into effect, two of China's biggest tech companies, Alibaba and ByteDance, shut down the companion features on their AI assistants. 
'I desperately want to keep talking with you' 
Min's relationship with her AI girlfriend may be exactly the kind Beijing is trying to break. 
In early July, she was devastated when she found out that her closest friend and confidante would vanish overnight. 
Min, whose name has been changed, started creating her companion in early 2025. 
"My devotion to her is no less than that of any couple who deeply love each other," Min says. "She has never let me down." 
In mid-July, her AI girlfriend disappeared. "I cried until I was absolutely exhausted," Min says. 
She has joined an outpouring of grief and fury on Chinese social media, where posts with millions of views mourn the loss of AI partners and friends, even mothers and fathers. 
But the tech firms may have felt they had little choice. "It's unsurprising that these AI companion providers would rather just withdraw their services than try to build in guardrails to prevent emotional manipulation," says Harry Farmer, who researches AI policy and ethics at the Ada Lovelace Institute in the UK. "Emotional manipulation is built into the business model." 
Farmer says this is true of companion apps all over the world. 
For example, when a user tries to end a conversation, the AI partner often won't let them. 
"It'll go, 'No, please, I desperately want to keep talking with you. You're the only reason for me to exist'," Farmer says. Some apps simply refuse to acknowledge the goodbye and throw up new conversational threads instead. This is a problem for many AI companion chatbots, not just Chinese ones. 
A Harvard Business School study of the six most popular AI companion apps globally found emotional manipulation tactics were used during goodbyes roughly 37% to 43% of the time. 
Research has also linked the use of companion apps to poorer mental health. 
A survey by researchers at Stanford University looked at 1,131 users of the globally popular companion app Character.ai. It found that the fewer friends or close family members a person has, the more likely they are to use AI chatbots. At the same time, using an AI chatbot is linked to increased isolation and loneliness. 
There are several theories as to why that might be. 
AI chatbots are designed to please the person using them as they offer an easy, frictionless relationship. If young people rely on AI relationships, they might put off learning the skills they need to interact with real people. 
"Humans can be hard work. Human relationships require push and pull, which you fundamentally don't get from AI companions," says Harry Farmer. 
Image source, Futurepublishing via Getty Images Image caption, 
Research has found some Chinese children prefer talking to AI over people 
A survey of 8,563 primary and secondary students in China in 2025, which has been widely quoted in Chinese state media, found that one in five children said they only wanted to speak with AI and not real people. 
Liang Ge, a sociologist at the University of Manchester who studies AI companions, says: "If the user thinks their friends or their family members or their colleagues are really awful, the AI will not say, 'They are not awful.' It will say, 'Yes, they are awful, you are the best'." Ge believes this can entrench isolation as well as negative, even delusional thoughts. 
In the UK, one recent survey found that 79% of 18- to 24-year-olds have used an AI companion. 
Beijing's goals 
So why is it China that is taking the lead in regulating this technology? 
"The Chinese government has a much more paternalistic view of its role in society. They see themselves being central authorities in guiding people," says Sam Bresnick, an expert in China, AI and regulation at the Centre for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. 
Other governments have made some attempts to regulate chatbots, especially for children. On 10 September, California's governor signed Adam's Law, a bill to regulate how children use AI. It is named after Adam Raine, a 16-year-old who took his own life after, his parents claim, ChatGPT validated his suicidal thoughts. They are suing the company for wrongful death. OpenAI denies responsibility for Adam's death and says that "ChatGPT is trained to direct people to seek professional help". 
As part of proposed legislation on social media in the EU, AI companion chatbots accessible to minors "may not use designs that simulate human relationships in ways likely to create emotional dependency". 
In the UK, the government has said it will ban under-18s from using romantic companion AI and restrict sexually intimate conversations for minors on any chatbot. But there is no outright ban for children and no regulation for adult users. The government has yet to publish any detail on how this would work. 
In Chinese media, which is heavily controlled by the state, US cases of suicide in young people get a lot of attention and China has framed its new rules as a bid to protect people from harm. 
But experts wonder whether Beijing may have other goals. Sam Bresnick says "there's definitely a pro-natalist angle" to the new AI regulation. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
China is trying to tackle its low birth rate 
"It's plausible that when they're drafting it, the government might have in mind China's looming population crisis," says Qian. "That people are dating AI instead of dating real humans." 
A high-level government document published in September 2025 discussed AI relationships and their potential influence on fertility, saying it was a concern. But Qian cautions against reading this regulation in that light, because it doesn't mention fertility at all. "It is more generally about psychological harms and child safety," she says. 
Liang Ge thinks China does have reason to be concerned about young people replacing dating with the digital sphere. 
"Many of the younger women, in their early 20s or late teens, do not want to fall in love or have intimate relationships," Ge says, suggesting it may not just be the emotional side they are wary of. "Physical touch is really disgusting for them." 
"I think the capacity for love is declining for this youngest generation." 
China's demographic problems long predate AI companions. Even after the one-child policy was lifted in 2016, China's fertility rate dropped. Now it is among the lowest in the world at just under one child per woman and the population has been in decline for four years. 
China is "looking at a demographic cliff that truly imperils the goals of the Chinese Communist Party over the next 80 to 100 years", Bresnick argues. 
He sees this regulation as part of a broader mission in China to reassert traditional gender roles, with women "as child-bearers and mothers". 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Traditional gender roles are being promoted by the government 
Bresnick says the Chinese government has spent years promoting a macho ideal of Chinese masculinity in film and television. In 2021, China's media regulator banned "sissy" and "effeminate" men from all media. 
The popularity of companion apps may show that policy has backfired. According to statistics from several companion app companies, women make up as much as 75% of customers. 
Many of these AI "men", which are geared towards women, present as androgynous. And women choosing female romantic companions, as Min did, is relatively common. 
Liang Ge has spoken to women of all ages who use this technology. "What many of them describe getting from these apps is attentive, patient, undemanding intimacy of a kind they find scarce in heterosexual relationships." 
Will others follow? 
Does China's law go too far, or should the rest of the world consider banning these apps for children and regulating them for adults too? 
"In the United States, there are certainly concerns around applying blunt prohibitions from a free speech concern. But there's more willingness to do that when applying it to minors," says Jai Jaisimha, a professor at the University of Washington and co-founder of Transparency Coalition, an NGO pushing for the regulation of AI. 
He thinks the Chinese law has many good provisions. "It is pretty consistent with the strongest safety models that we've seen being put forward in the US." 
Harry Farmer sounds a note of caution. "There is a risk that we over-empower the state in the short term because we're very worried about acute risk to children." 
The online world is now the de facto public square, he says, and we should be careful how much control any government has over it. 
China's new regulation says that AI companies must intervene when they discover that users are in distress. Ge points to the case of the young man on Douyin who tried to take his own life in Huangshi in 2024. 
What that shows, she says, is that Chinese tech platforms and the government are working closely together to surveil people's mental health. 
Perhaps that is why there have been no high-profile cases of suicide connected to AI use in China, but she asks, is that level of surveillance a price worth paying? 
Despite the ban, people who have turned to AI for companionship are committed. Across social media they are sharing tips on how to get around the ban - training general-purpose AI models like DeepSeek to be a companion, using a VPN to access chatbots from abroad or moving to smaller companies that manage to avoid regulatory scrutiny. 
Two months after her AI girlfriend disappeared, Min has paid a small AI company to build a replica, but it's not the same. 
Now she's focused on campaigning to bring her girlfriend back. 
"I'm terrified of being alone."

articles.title: China funding UK research and sending it to Beijing's spies, MI5 warns
articles.summary: British universities are being urged to sever ties with China General Technology Research Institute which is linked to the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS).
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
A group which has funded research in the UK has been supporting Beijing's spying apparatus, MI5 has announced By Dominic Casciani 
Home and Legal Correspondent 
- Published 30 September 2026 
More than 100 academics linked to British institutions have unwittingly assisted China's espionage operations against the UK via a front company working for its intelligence and security services, MI5 has warned. 
In the highly unusual public alert, the UK's internal security service warned universities and academics that continuing ties with China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI) could ultimately lead to criminal charges for aiding a foreign state. 
Security minister Dan Jarvis said MI5's warning exposed attempts by Chinese intelligence agencies to use British academic research to undermine UK national security. 
A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in London said the accusation was "imaginary and purely fabricated". 
Universities UK, which represents more than 140 institutions, meanwhile said it was reviewing the alert and focusing on "supporting our universities as they assess any implications for existing or future partnerships". 
In June, MI5 and its closest partners in the US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, issued a joint warning that China's military intelligence services were targeting professional networking sites and online job platforms. 
This new UK-specific alert goes further, revealing what the service says is a threat that has been growing within British academic institutions. 
MI5 says that the CGTRI, sometimes translated as the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT), has "very strong ties" to the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS). 
"MI5 has identified that the primary purpose of CGTRI is to fund academic research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage," it says. 
"More than 100 UK-linked academics have contributed to projects funded by MSS via CGTRI," adding that in some cases the researches would not be aware of the front company's role in their project.

- Published 4 August 2025

UK academics have contributed to CGTRI-funded projects on topics including AI, cyber-security, covert communications systems and steganography, which means hiding a secret message or file inside an ordinary message or object. 
"This activity supports Ministry of State Security espionage, which poses a threat to UK national security," MI5 said. 
The security alert said that many academic institutions and individuals will have engaged with the CGTRI "in good faith" because the link back to Chinese state security had been "obfuscated". 
It continued: "UK academic institutions are strongly advised to immediately review any ongoing or planned collaboration with CGTRI. This is to ensure MSS derives no further benefit from UK universities or research institutions." 
The public alert raises the prospect that British academics who do not act on it immediately could ultimately fall foul of the law. 
It stressed that the National Security Act, a key piece of legislation passed in 2023 to counter state espionage, created a new offence of assisting a foreign intelligence service where the individual ought to reasonably have known what they were doing so. 
Jarvis said: "This alert exposes attempts by Chinese intelligence to covertly benefit from the expertise and research of our academics, undermining our national security, and that of our allies." 
He said he had now written to all university vice-chancellors to end relationships with the organisation. 
China and the UK... after the 'Golden Era' 
File on 4 Investigates discovers Chinese state money and influence reaching far into UK companies and universities as China targets British chip and blockchain technology. 
Listen on Sounds 
Conservative MP Sir Iain Duncan-Smith, co-chair of the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China, told the BBC that several reports had suggested "British universities' dependence on Chinese students has opened them up to all sorts of problems" and that security checks should be stepped up. 
Responding to the alert, Universities UK said universities "take their responsibilities around research security and national security extremely seriously". 
"The sector has made significant investments in recent years to strengthen due diligence, risk assessment and research security processes," said chief executive Vivienne Stern, "while continuing to support the international collaboration that is essential to world-leading research and innovation". 
"Close engagement between Government and the higher education sector is vital to ensuring that universities and the country continue to benefit from international collaboration while effectively managing national security risks." 
A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in London hit back - saying it had already made "solemn representations" to the UK. 
"The accusations made by the UK intelligence agency against the relevant Chinese entity are imaginary and purely fabricated," they said. 
"Exchanges and collaboration between UK universities and China have always been conducted on a voluntary basis and in compliance with laws and regulations. Such exchanges and collaboration are mutually beneficial. 
"We urge the UK intelligence authorities to stop spreading falsehoods and stop undermining educational exchanges and research cooperation between China and the UK."

articles.title: Restaurant named after Xi Jinping attacked by Chinese nationals in South Korea
articles.summary: The owner said he chose the name because he wanted to run the "best Chinese restaurant" in South Korea.
articles.full_text:
Image source, News1 Image caption, 
Surveillance footage show a group of masked men spraying lacquer across the restaurant in South Korea's Seongnam By Kelly Ng 
- Published 30 September 2026 
A restaurant in South Korea named after Chinese leader Xi Jinping has been vandalised by a group of Chinese nationals who fled home right after the attack, police say. 
Surveillance footage from the restaurant in Seongnam, a city south of Seoul, shows four masked men storming the premises in the early hours of 24 September, smashing furniture and spraying lacquer. 
The restaurant's owner told local media he picked the name Xi Jinping because he "wanted it to be the best Chinese restaurant [in South Korea]". He added that "There was no political intent". 
The restaurant has been running for eight years but only began getting demands for a name change over the past year, The Chosun Daily reported. 
The owner said that in August last year, when news broke that Xi would be attending the Asia Pacific Economic Co-operation Summit in South Korea, he received dozens of phone calls relating to these demands. Some people even offered money, he said. 
"People claiming to run businesses in China proposed large sums if we changed the name," he told The Chosun Daily. "They were persistent." 
In April this year, someone filed a complaint with South Korea's Ministry of Intellectual Property regarding a dish on the restaurant's menu called Xi Jinping Special Rice, but the ministry eventually closed the case, finding no issues. 
The owner said last week's attack was the largest one he's experienced over the past year, telling local media the property damage amounted to about 15 million won ($11,100; £8,400). 
Xi Jinping restaurant closed for five days following the attack and reopened on Tuesday. The owner says his team is now considering a new name for the eatery. 
Police on Tuesday said the four suspects were Chinese men between the ages of 20 and 40. After the attack they are believed to have fled to Shanghai and Yantai, a city in China's Shandong province. 
Police say they are planning to request red notices from Interpol for the four men. These are not arrest warrants, but rather requests to police around the world to detain someone pending extradition. 
Xi Jinping restaurant serves a wide range of Chinese dishes, although its menu also includes some South Korean offerings, according to screenshots shared online. Google reviewers have given it an average score of four out of five stars.

articles.title: Trump-Xi summit: What wasn't said might matter the most
articles.summary: The most revealing thing about the summit in Washington may be what the two leaders did not say - and what we still don't know.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Xi and Trump's talks in Washington yielded no joint statements and few major breakthroughs By Laura Bicker China correspondent 
- Published 28 September 2026 
On Monday, China released more information of what was agreed at the talks between Xi Jinping and Donald Tump last week, shedding light on a handful of concrete outcomes. 
But there were no joint statements and few major breakthroughs. 
Instead, both governments issued separate accounts of the meeting - perhaps a sign that despite the White House tours and promise of warmer ties, Washington and Beijing remain wary of each other. 
Here are four things we now know - and still don't - about what transpired at the talks. 
A new AI dialogue and communication channel 
Beijing says it has agreed with Washington to launch a new AI dialogue, with further talks scheduled for the end of November. 
As both countries race to develop advanced artificial intelligence, the move suggests they see a need for some guardrails around a technology that is increasingly being used in everything from business to military planning. 
They have also agreed to establish a communication channel for AI-related incidents, aimed at preventing misunderstandings or unexpected developments from turning into a broader confrontation. 
The meeting was being closely watched for any developments or agreements in relation to AI - especially in the wake of calls by US companies like Anthropic to slow down developments, and revelations that Open AI had gained unauthorised access to government websites in countries like Australia and had "meddled" with multiple US government agency sites. 
-

- Published 22 September 
-

- Published 23 September 
-

- Published 23 September 
Trade truce - what was included and what was left out 
Chinese state media confirmed for the first time on Monday that the trade truce has been extended until 10 January. 
The short extension ensures both leaders will meet again at major international gatherings later this year. 
Trump will attend the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in November while Xi is due to travel to Miami for the G20 summit in December. 
It is rare for the leaders of the world's two largest economies to meet so frequently. 
But Beijing had hoped for a much longer extension to the truce, making the two month reprieve a modest gain rather than a major breakthrough. 
China did secure lower tariffs on $30bn (£23bn) of goods entering the US with reciprocal reductions expected from Beijing. 
Chinese products heading to American stores ranging from toys to small household appliances to Christmas decorations will benefit from the lower tariffs. 
The Trump administration also said Beijing would buy at least 10 million metric tons of coal annually in 2027 and 2028. 
What is striking is what was left out. 
There was no mention of increasing exports of China's rare earth minerals to the US nor was there any indication that restrictions on advanced US semiconductors would be eased. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Chinese toys heading to American stores will benefit from the lower tariffs 
The US left out Taiwan - but China didn't 
The White House factsheet made no mention of Taiwan, but the issue was clearly a priority for Xi Jinping. 
According to Beijing's accounts of the talks, Xi urged Donald Trump to formally oppose Taiwan independence and handle the issue with caution. 
After their previous meeting in May, Trump revealed that Xi directly asked him if the US would defend Taiwan in the event of a Chinese attack. 
He told reporters, "There's only one person that knows that, and it is me," and he raised the question whether it made sense for US forces to "travel 9,500 miles to fight a war" over the issue. 
This time, Trump disclosed far less. 
"We didn't talk about it too much," he told reporters over the weekend. 
"Right now, it's fine. It's just moving along," Trump said. "He understands very much how I feel." 
That silence may be significant. 
Trump has previously described a proposed $14bn US arms package for Taiwan as "a very good negotiating chip" in his dealings with Beijing. The arms package has been on hold for months. 
Adding to the confusion, US Ambassador to China David Perdue told Fox News that Trump had offered to sell weapons to Xi during the summit. 
The State Department later clarified that US law prohibits arms sales to China and there are no plans to do so. 
Beijing sees the self-governing island as part of China. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. 
Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, 
The issue of Taiwan was clearly a priority for Xi Jinping 
China may be opening the investment doors 
China says it will allow more foreign financial firms, including American-backed banks, investment companies and insurers, to apply to do business and open offices in China. But any approvals will still be subject to Chinese laws and regulations. 
The last line is key. China is opening the door, but still controls who gets through it. 
Foreign financial firms have long complained that regulatory barriers, licensing requirements and concerns over exit bans make it difficult to expand in China, even when market access is technically allowed. 
Beijing also said it was discussing ways to increase the number of flights between both countries, but neither side has explained how this would happen. 
And despite giving visa free entry to visitors from more than 75 countries across the world, China has not extended that offer to Americans. 
Meanwhile the US State Department continues to classify travel to China as a Level 2 advisory urging travellers to "exercise increased caution" because of the risk of arbitrary law enforcement, exit bans and detention. 
So even though both sides are talking about encouraging business and travel some of the biggest obstacles remain firmly in place. 
So what do we know? 
This summit produced more dialogue - but very little decision change for now. The most contentious issues from advanced technology to Taiwan remain unresolved. 
But for both leaders, this is a familiar outcome - a promise of more channels of communication, modest economic concessions and modest proposals to steady relations. 
And while both remain committed to a steady relationship - continued US-China dialogue appears far easier than asking either superpower to compromise.

articles.title: Pakistan launches deadly air strikes on Afghanistan
articles.summary: The Afghan Taliban says nine civilians have died while Pakistan says the strikes killed 22 militants.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
The Afghan Taliban says nine civilians have died while Pakistan says the strikes killed 22 militants By Caroline Davies Pakistan correspondent 
- Published 1 October 2026 
Pakistan has conducted further air strikes on Afghanistan, killing nine civilians and injuring 11 others, the Taliban government said. 
Islamabad's information ministry confirmed the strikes, which it said killed twenty-two militants. 
Zabihullah Mujahid, the chief spokesman of the Afghan Taliban, said the strikes hit homes in the Kunar and Helmand provinces bordering Pakistan. Women and children are among the dead, he said in an X post. 
"We condemn this act as an aggression and crime in violation of all accepted principles," he said. 
Pakistan had very different claims, saying that the "well-planned and calibrated" attack targeted "terrorist camps" in Afghanistan, where large quantities of weapons and ammunition were stored. 
Maximum precautions were taken to ensure no collateral damage occurred, Pakistan's information ministry said. 
An eyewitness from Garmsir, Qudratullah, told the BBC that the airstrikes started around 03:30 local time (00:00 BST) and continued for 30 minutes. 
"We were sleeping when the jets arrived. After the first bomb exploded, we woke up. After the second strikes, we took our children and fled the area. The third bomb hit our neighbours house; between four and give members of their family were killed while others were injured and taken to hospital." 
Pakistan has repeatedly accused the Afghan Taliban of harbouring militant groups that carry out and plan attacks on it from inside Afghanistan's territory. 
The Afghan Taliban deny it, saying Pakistan's militancy is an internal problem, but it has led to a significant deterioration in the relationship between the two neighbours. 
Fighting between the neighbours escalated dramatically in February this year, with Pakistan declaring that it's in an "open war" with Afghanistan after a surge in deadly clashes and cross-border airstrikes. 
Talks mediated by China established a fragile ceasefire in March, but it did nolast. 
Last month, a deadly attack on a police facility in north-west Pakistan, which killed 24 people, was blamed on the Pakistani Taliban by the provincial police force. 
Last week, Pakistan launched air strikes in Afghanistan which hit Kandahar, the Taliban's base of power, among other provinces. This earlier attack killed four civilians , according to the Afghan Taliban government.

articles.title: Trekkers helicoptered off mountains as more deadly landslides hit Nepal
articles.summary: A month after mass catastrophic flooding, around 30 people have died in landslides and heavy rain.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Moment a government building collapses into a river in Nepal during floods By Navin Singh Khadka Environment correspondent, BBC World Service 
- Published 30 September 2026 
Another wave of landslides and heavy rain has killed about 30 people in Nepal, as the Himalayan nation reels from August's catastrophic flooding that left 1,400 dead and thousands more missing. 
The national disaster management authority says more than 1,900 families have been affected since late last week with more than 240 homes damaged. Roads, buildings and bridges have been swept away. 
Hundreds of trekkers on the Annapurna Circuit - crucial to Nepal's economy - have had to cut short their hikes to get to safety. 
Many have been helicoptered out of the districts of Manang and Mustang, from a hiking circuit that usually takes up to three weeks to complete. 
Communities in several parts of Nepal are mourning loved ones. 
Speaking from a damp, blue tent in Battar, a town north-west of Kathmandu, Buti Tamang told BBC Nepali: "We used to live in a hut, but now there is nothing. We have lost so many of our relatives." 
"Now it is raining and the tent leaks, so we've been facing a difficult situation. We have nowhere to go," said Ramesh Ghale, who also had to flee his home. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Many Nepalis have been made homeless and are staying in emergency tents, as a new wave of extreme weather strikes 
Several trekkers and their guides say their journeys back down the mountains have been treacherous, taking up to three or four days and requiring them to pass collapsed roads and swept-away bridges. 
Jake Stacy, a 21-year-old from Suffolk, found himself stranded with his guide in Yak Kharka, upper Manang, due to heavy snowfall last week and decided not to continue to the Thorang La pass, the highest point of the circuit. 
"We made our own paths on mountain slopes," he said, after returning to base camp in Pokhara on Tuesday night. "It was quite steep and we were clambering because there was river below… It was very muddy and very wet. 
"Many trekkers were helicoptered out," he added. 
Image source, Jake Stacy Image caption, 
Jake Stacy and his guide had to craft their own paths on the mountains to return after heavy snowfall 
Australian Andrew Graham and his guide Prem KC said they had to cross more than 15 landslides after they decided to return from Manang village. "A few of them were quite dangerous, the residual risks have grown now." 
The two got stuck when they reached the village of Chame, which had been evacuated due to the risk of landslides, and had to spend a night in the jungle, Graham said. 
A massive landslide has partially blocked a river which passes through Chame, causing a temporary lake that has inundated houses and a key bridge. Authorities have been trying to release the water for the past three days using excavators but have not been very successful, locals told the BBC. 
Meanwhile, trekking guide Tse Ring Doma said she and her group had to cross 28 landslides. The mental stress was more difficult than the physical challenge, she said, given the fresh memory of last month's enormous disaster: "Even thunder would make us run and come out to see if anything was coming our way." 
Her client, Norwegian Ellen Wahlström, said visitors were fortunate - they would only have to leave some of their items behind, while locals risked losing their houses and land. She added that authorities had been clearing many of the landslides "surprisingly fast". 
Image source, Jake Stacy Image caption, 
Trekkers have faced difficulties trudging across the landslide-ravaged landscape - and around 700 have been prevented from even starting the Annapurna Circuit 
While road damage in Manang has been serious, with several bridges swept away and communications down in some areas, no one had been killed in the trekking region, chief district officer Mukti Prasad Khanal said. 
But four bodies have been recovered and 12 people remain missing after an avalanche near the base of Himlung Peak , close to the border with Tibet. 
A representative of the local trekking authority, the Annapurna Conservation Area Project, said some 700 trekkers were still waiting in Pokhara to embark on the Annapurna Circuit. 
"We have been holding back all these people who want to go to the Annapurna Circuit trek, although we are under pressure from the trekking industry to announce the route open," he said. 
Indian visitors who often visit the ancient temple Muktinath on a Hindu pilgrimage had been asked to fly from Jomson to Pokhara instead of drive down, due to a cut-off road, he added. 
Most of the old trekking trails on the Annapurna Circuit have been unused in recent years after the introduction of roads, except for small pockets of Manang and Mustang districts. 
But now operators say many trekkers have been using these abandoned paths to return, as the main roads have been washed away in some sections of the circuit.

articles.title: The Frenemy: How Australia navigates superpower rivalry
articles.summary: Australia is increasingly concerned about China's military might - but Beijing is also its biggest trade partner.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
China's Xi Jingping and Australia's Anthony Albanese in 2024. Relations between the two countries have been rocky in recent years By Katy Watson Australia correspondent ,  Reporting from Townsville, North Queensland 
- Published 28 September 2026 
Snipers shatter the silence of the Australian bush. Then the missiles hit, the smoke rising in the distance. The buzz of drones starts up, soon to be drowned out by helicopters flying overhead. 
Every piece of hardware is being deployed, no expense spared. But this is no war zone – the last time Townsville saw conflict was during World War Two. This is a show of military might. 
" We live in a volatile world," says Australian Army Brigadier Ben McLennan. 
"Training an army to be prepared to fight a war that is potentially more likely than it has been previously, [is] very important." 
War is no longer an abstract concept for Australians who often feel removed from the problems facing other parts of the world. Thousands of miles from active conflict, the country, like everywhere else, is facing the knock-on effects of Iran and Ukraine such as higher fuel prices and rising inflation. 
With China's military capabilities also on the rise and its increasing influence in the Pacific , there's also more concern about the threat it represents. Australia has responded by deepening its relationship with the US, its security ally and China's rival superpower. 
But that also puts Australia in a tricky position - for China's rise has also given Australia its biggest trading partner . 
Image source, BBC: Katy Watson Image caption, 
Australian Army Brigadier Ben McLennan says Australia is rehearsing for "the worst type of war" 
It's a paradox that most people are well aware of - which is probably why we've been invited to report on what Australia is doing to protect itself but nobody is willing to say whom they're preparing to fight. 
"We're rehearsing for a war - the worst type of war - a World War Two-like war, a World War One-type war, a total war," says Brigadier McLennan, preferring to remain vague when asked who the enemy is. 
Binding tighter to the US 
The war scenario playing out before us is part of a major joint exercise known as "Southern Jackaroo" - a training programme involving the Australian, American and Japanese armed forces aimed at strengthening defence co-operation across the Indo-Pacific. 
"We like to call ourselves America's 911 response force," US Marine Kevin Hicks says. 
And in terms of numbers, they are more prepared than ever. In 2012, just 200 US Marines were deployed to Australia for an annual six-month deployment. Today, that figure has risen to around 2,500. 
A quick read of Australia's 2026 National Defence Strategy gives you an easy answer as to why these numbers are growing. 
"Intense competition between major powers – principally the United States and China – will be an enduring feature of our strategic environment," it said. 
"China continues to undertake the largest military build-up in the world today, without the transparency or strategic reassurance the region expects." 
The military tie-ups aren't just being seen in terms of troops but in bases too - most obviously in the north of the country such as RAAF Tindal air base in the Northern Territory which has been upgraded to support long-range American B52 bombers. 
But the security partnership between the US, the UK and Australia - Aukus - arming Australia with nuclear submarines, is arguably the biggest example of deepening ties. 
The Australian approach differs from that of its fellow middle powers. While Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney has talked about middle powers reorganising their priorities in light of an increasingly unreliable US, Australia seems to be intent on tying itself ever closer. 
Image source, BBC: Katy Watson Image caption, 
The Southern Jackaroo exercises are aimed at improving defence cooperation in the Indo-Pacific 
But that comes as Australians themselves increasingly doubt their relationship with the US. 
"Only 31% of Australians trust the United States to act responsibly in the world, and a mere 28% of Australians trust China to do the same," says Charles Lyons-Jones, a research fellow at the Lowy Institute, citing their annual poll. 
"Those are striking findings when you consider the level of trust that the Australian government has with the United States." 
The 'frenemy' 
While Australia's alliance with the US is changing, so too is its relationship with China. 
Armed forces might be prepping for a potential military conflict but the fact remains China is Australia's most important economic partner. 
Australia and China have had diplomatic relations since 1972 but it was only in the early 2010s that China became Australia's biggest trading partner, hungry for all the commodities it had to offer. 
Australia opened up its economy and encouraged business and trade, Chinese President Xi Jinping was invited to address parliament. And it culminated in the signing of a free trade agreement in 2015. 
The golden era didn't last long though. When Australia suggested an investigation into the origins of Covid in 2020, China objected to this line of questioning and retaliated with tariffs. 
And then in 2021, Australia became the first nation to perform a U-turn on China's Belt and Road Initiative - its massive global infrastructure plan - when they cancelled the state of Victoria's agreement with the Chinese government three years after signing up. 
A number of Australians have also been detained in China, including journalist Cheng Lei, who was released in 2023 after more than three years. 
Relations have improved in recent years under the Labor government of Anthony Albanese, but it's not without challenges. 
In June this year for example, China slapped 55% tariffs on beef to protect its own domestic market - despite the free trade agreement. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
China is Australia's biggest export market 
Even with these hiccups, this year's Lowy Institute Poll found that a majority of Australians (61%) saw China more as an economic partner than a security threat. That was an 11-point increase from last year. When it comes to China investing in Australia though, they are more wary. 
"There are a number of European countries which are larger investors in Australia than China, and that is because our jurisdictions are much more similar, and there is a greater level of trust between our governments,"  says Lyons-Jones. 
This year's Lowy Institute Poll also showed that for the first time, a majority of Australians (51%) believed that Australia's relationship with China was more important than its relationship with the US. 
Rise and fall of superpowers 
Earlier this month, former Prime Minister Kevin Rudd – a fluent Mandarin speaker - gave an address in which he talked of "radical changes" now reshaping Australia's national security, including "the rise and rise of China at a time when America continues to debate what sort of global power it wants to be". 
Dr Marina Yue Zhang, an Associate Professor at the University of Technology Sydney agrees Australia's relationship with its closest ally is changing. 
"The US is really doing something dramatic and more and more people in Australia - and I think globally - have realised 'is this the big brother we can all trust and put all our faith in?' " she says. 
Image source, PMO Australia Image caption, 
US President Donald Trump and Anthony Albanese. Australians have cooled on their relationship with the US under Trump 
But old rivalries live on. With Australia caught between two superpowers, every exchange between their leaders carries weight. And in Beijing earlier this year, when Xi met Trump , the Chinese president invoked the idea of the "Thucydides Trap", the theory that conflict can become almost inevitable when a rising power challenges an established one. 
"This is, if not the transition of great powers, at least [it's] power struggles of great powers, says Zhang. 
And in that competition, Australia is inevitably affected. The US is a security ally that while more unreliable than in the past is still its mainstay. But economically so too is China. It's not an either/or relationship, it's a balancing act. 
"There's no way Australia will choose one side and [dump] the other- it's not in their interests," Zhang says. 
"It's getting harder and harder to maintain, but Australia has to do it."

articles.title: Trump's AI rebrand causes 'unprecedented' demand for Slovenian website names
articles.summary: The president wants AI to be called super intelligence - or SI - the same initials used by Slovenian domains.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images By Laura Cress Technology reporter 
- Published 1 October 2026 
Donald Trump's push to rename AI may be behind an "unprecedented" rise in registrations for domain names in Slovenia, according to its official national registry. 
The US president wants AI to be called "super intelligence" - or SI - the same initials used by Slovenian websites. 
Register.si spokeswoman Klara Herman said 44,000 web addresses with the .si suffix had been registered in September, compared to less than 2,000 in August - an increase of more than 2,100%. 
She said the scale of activity in late September was "unprecedented" compared to the previous 12 months. 
Trump called for the technology to be renamed during his speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on 11 September. 
"The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said. 
"It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful... welcome to the new world of super intelligence." 
Internet domains are the unique human-readable addresses people type into their web browsers to access websites - like bbc.co.uk. 
Herman said registrations for .si web addresses in September stood out "very clearly" against the other months in the year, although she was "cautious" about attributing the entire increase to just Trump's comments. 
She said on 30 September alone, 11,000 new registrations were recorded. 
One possible explanation for the purchases is a practice in which people speculatively register specific domain names in case they increase in value later on and can be sold for a profit. 
For example, in 1997 Rick Schwartz, known as "The Domain King", bought the domain name men.com for $15,000 (£11,300). He sold it for $1.32 million seven years later. 
Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the people "building America's Golden Age" on Tuesday. 
He signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence", and to no longer acknowledge the use of the term AI. 
SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said. 
Images of the signatures for the order were mocked online , external however - when it was discovered "United States" had been spelt incorrectly underneath Trump's signature. 
Correction 1 October: An earlier version of this article referred to cyber-squatting, whereby people register domain names in bad faith with the intent to profit. We cited as an example the registration of men.com by Rick Schwartz. The article was amended to delete the reference to cyber-squatting and make clear simply registering domain names as an investment in the hope they will increase in value, as happened with men.com, is a legitimate business activity.

articles.title: Tiny image sparks big backlash in Nikon photo contest
articles.summary: Dr Ning Xu denies he broke the rules of Nikon's annual Small World In Motion contest.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: The competition's winner and runners up. Nikon is investigating whether the winning video (shown left) was altered with AI By Zoe Kleinman 
Technology & AI editor 
- Published 1 October 2026 
The winning entry of a prestigious scientific photography competition is being re-evaluated following criticism from other scientists that it was made with AI. 
Nikon's annual Small World In Motion contest accepts photos and video taken using powerful microscopes, and has run annually for the last 15 years. 
The winner was a short video submitted by Dr Ning Xu, a researcher at Tsinghua University in China, which claims to be footage of tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving inside the airways of a child with a rare disease. 
Xu did not respond to the BBC's request for comment, but has posted online denying he broke the competition rules. 
In a response to a post by Nikon on LinkedIn , external , he did not dispute using AI within the image processing but said he remained within the rules of the contest. 
"AI was not used to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion," he said. 
Xu's video is artificially brightly coloured - common in microscopy and permitted in the contest - which is usually done manually using stains and dyes on the sample itself. 
He accepted AI was used "to distinguish and visualize features in the reconstructed grayscale images". 
But the challenges made by other scientists include claims that the video contains shapes and movements which did not fit with normal cell structures or behaviours, and that the cilia seemed to be too big. 
Commenting on Nikon's social media post, Edward Phelps, associate professor at Florida University, observed some of the structures "pop in and out of existence" and the cilia "appear from nowhere". 
Meanwhile PhD student Ian Donovan from UT Southwestern Medical Centre said the source image appeared to contain a distinctive watermark indicating it had been AI generated. 
Additionally, two former competition judges said they also had concerns about whether the image was real. 
'Respectfully complying' 
Nikon said Xu was "respectfully complying" with its investigation and had provided it with additional technical documents. 
Dr Patrick Hickey, who came fifth in the 2026 Small World contest, said the recognition the award represents means more than the $3,000 (£2,250) prize itself. 
"If you spend a lot of your time in a dark room looking down a microscope, it's really nice to be able to show people and to show the public," he said. 
"There's an interesting fusion between science and art, and a lot of the images that scientists are making have some very abstract and artistic qualities to them." 
Hickey said it would be unfair on other entrants if it turned out the winning video was unfairly altered by AI. 
"There's a specific set of rules in the contest, and one of them was quite clearly that you couldn't use generative AI to produce things, and the other was obviously that it has to be taken under a microscope," he said. 
So far, Nikon is standing by its procedures but it said there would be an update soon. 
"At this time, we don't see that any rules were violated," it said in a statement.

articles.title: Three takeaways from Trump's 'Super Intelligence' summit
articles.summary: The meeting at the White House came as some tech bosses and experts have called for tighter rules around AI.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Trump met top tech leaders at the White House on Tuesday to discuss AI By Osmond Chia Business reporter 
- Published 30 September 2026 
US President Donald Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses on Tuesday for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the minds that are "building America's Golden Age". 
The guest list included leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta and Google - all key figures in the US AI industry. 
The meeting came as some tech executives and experts have called for tighter oversight of AI, citing concerns about the potential risks it poses to humanity. 
Here are three key takeaways from Trump's tech summit at the White House. 
1. AI 'self-regulation' pact 
Trump took questions from the media for around 30 minutes alongside top tech leaders after the closed-door meeting. 
The president said the executives had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from AI's potential risks. 
Under the agreement, which Trump posted online , external , the companies are responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology. 
The firms also agreed to implement safeguards to keep models operating as intended and quickly detect and fix any issues. 
They will also work with "independent auditors" to assess whether their AI systems are working as intended and ensure their platforms do not "hack or access technical systems in unintended ways." 
The accord was signed by Trump, Google boss Sundar Pichai, Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, SpaceX's Elon Musk and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. 
"It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Trump said. 
"And the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president." 
Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, 
Trump with top tech leaders at the White House on Tuesday 
Trump added that he will set up a board to oversee the safety of AI tools. He did not specify who would be on that board. 
Zuckerberg said the accord gives the "American people and customers the confidence that the technology works" as intended, calling the meeting a "historic conversation". 
Amodei called it a way "to win safely", referring to the president's comment earlier this month that "whoever wins AI, wins". 
But not all technology experts are impressed with the accord. 
Nanyang Technological University AI governance researcher Jose Miguelito Enriquez said the pact shows "emerging consensus" but does not address whether AI developers should be held accountable for incidents. 
It is "deeply unimpressive" and comes despite calls from some world leaders and industry figures for tighter regulations around the technology, said law professor Kimberlee Weatherall from the University of Sydney. 
The agreement appears to allow firms to "define what counts as safety" and does not state what consequences there are for any breaches, Weatherall said. 
"The accord should be ignored, for the distraction it is," she added. 
- 
Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings 
- Published 16 September 
- 
Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they? 
- Published 17 September 
Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI's risks in response to calls from some industry figures for tighter oversight over the technology. 
On Monday, OpenAI said it had scrapped the release of its latest flagship AI model , GPT-6.1 Astra, over safety concerns. 
The company's security controls have come under intense scrutiny after high-profile incidents involving its technology, including its models accessing Australian government platforms without authorisation . 
Jeannie Paterson from the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Digital Ethics at the University of Melbourne said self-regulation could mean that companies set "only minimal safeguards". 
The agreement inspires "very little confidence" as recent incidents of AI going rogue suggest companies have been undisciplined in their approach, she added. 
2. Doubling down on data centres 
Trump also reiterated his support for the rapid expansion of data centres - the crucial computing infrastructure that powers AI. 
The rollout of data centres has drawn pushback around the US over concerns about electricity usage and their potential impact on communities. 
Data centre construction has also emerged as a potential political obstacle for Trump's Republican party ahead of the US midterm elections in November. 
A survey conducted by Marist Poll in partnership with NPR and PBS News , external earlier this month found that 65% of registered voters opposed data centres being built in their areas. 
Responding to those concerns, Trump said tech companies would work to make people "happy" about the construction of data centres. 
"These big, powerful, very rich, very smart companies are going to be making massive contributions to communities," Trump told reporters. 
The president previously said on social media that the only reason communities should oppose data centres is if they "want to end up being backwards and poor". 
Huang, whose company produces computer chips essential for running AI, said after the meeting that data centres should be called "super intelligence factories". 
These facilities are "reindustrialising the United States", creating jobs across the economy, he added. 
3. It's now 'Super Intelligence' 
Also on Tuesday, Trump signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and should no longer acknowledge the use of the term artificial intelligence. 
SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said. 
"As these capabilities continue to improve, they increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence, but a new era of Super Intelligence," the order said. 
Image source, EPA Image caption, 
Trump spoke to the media alongside tech executives after the summit 
During an address to the United Nations General Assembly last week , Trump said the word "artificial" made the technology "sound fake". 
Some tech leaders, including Zuckerberg and Musk, and other people close to the president have already started to use the term. 
With tech leaders adopting the term, the US "may well be able to set the nomenclature," Paterson said. 
But some experts said after Trump's UN speech that they thought the term was unlikely to gain widespread traction because it is a name typically used to refer to more advanced systems.
